<reason>CON won by making the motion's word "enough" the decision rule and forcing PRO to weigh against it. CON's opening ("a promise, not a car") set up a plausible night-supply arithmetic and a distinct verification failure mode; PRO's rebuttal that the timeout rider "never needed the button" narrowed PRO's own case to the invisible woman, which CON then attacked: for her, "no drivers available" delivers nothing, and universal tools may shrink the population who stay inside. In the pressure round both sides asked sharp questions, but CON answered honestly with a concrete standard (most 2 a.m. requests convert within comparable wait) and conceded PIN-matching doesn't restore a categorically refused trip, while PRO offered "any rate above zero," which CON devastatingly reduced to "one car per city per month." PRO's strongest live route — universal tools cannot create rides she refuses — stayed real, and the "lottery she cannot lose" line was memorable, but CON neutralized it by showing the platform pays every night while gains arrive "sometimes," and PRO's own concession of selfie re-verification became the added complexity in question. PRO never squarely handled the cost-center/litigation point beyond asserting a "false budget." CON adapted, narrowed, and weighed; PRO largely restated.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B2.3 turning PRO's "she can cancel, as she already can for a slow van" into proof that the filter's marginal contribution on most nights is delay — cancelling a slow van yields a normal car, cancelling a women-only wait yields the very pairing she wanted to avoid, later and tired — combined with B4.2's exploitation of PRO's "any rate above zero" threshold as a refusal to weigh "enough."</best_rebuttal>
